newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian protest newspaper a sellout success.
newsitem.headline: Belgian protest newspaper a sellout success.

text.p: A newspaper launched by Belgium's White March movement, which grew out of a protest by more than 250,000 people against child murders and police bungling, is turning into a runaway success.

Some 80,000 copies of the first edition of The White March, which costs 20 francs ($0.70), were snapped up in two days and another 100,000 are being printed, the movement's coordination office said on Thursday.
"It has far exceeded our expectations. We have touched the whole country," a spokeswoman who asked to be identified only as "Janie", told Reuters.
Belgium is in shock from Paedophile scandals with five young girls found dead and a hunt going on for others.
One idea floated in the first edition of the monthly is to hold another mass meeting next October 20 to found a national movement for change.
On Thursday 500 youngsters and the parents of some of the missing children planted 300 silver birch saplings to start a commemorative wood midway between Brussels and Antwerp.
The monthly White March newspaper is for people to air their views about failures of the justice system in the child disappearances, tell their stories and air their hopes.
"The purpose of this paper is not to be a vehicle for national bile," journalist Michel Lefevre said. "It is not to say everything is ruined. It is to say this is a new beginning."
The scandal came to a head in August when convicted child rapist Marc Dutroux led police to two captive girls who had been sexually abused and then to the bodies of four others.
The discoveries led to the October 20 "white march" that shook the political system and joined Belgium's French and Dutch speakers in a common cause to express deep anger.
The body of a fifth child was discovered in Brussels in February. Convicted child molester Patrick Derochette has been charged with illegal imprisonment and rape leading to the death of a minor.
A special parliamentary commission has seen 110 witnesses -- from magistrates to police and parents -- to try to find out what went wrong with the investigations.
It will report to parliament on April 15 and is expected to name some names.
Police are still searching for at least six other children who have gone missing in the last seven years.
On Thursday they began clearing a house in Dion on the border with France in connection with the disappearance in Brussels in December 1989 of 12-year-old Elizabeth Brichet.

The house belonged to amateur film-maker Jean-Marc Houdmont, who was killed in a car crash last month on the way to meet investigators with what he had told them by telephone was important information.
His companion, Monique Cherton, has been charged as an accomplice in abduction and illegal imprisonment.
There are now more than 100 White March committees scattered round Belgium, and there are small marches almost every weekend.
The next is due to take place at the coastal resort of De Panne on Easter Sunday. Upwards of 5,000 people are expected.
The government has promised changes, particularly to the parole system for convicted paedophiles, police coordination in investigations and support for victims and their families.
Dutroux and Derochette were both released early from their prison terms.
